blocks.text: Embedded Methods introduced the genuine general idea, feature selection emerging as a direct byproduct of a single model training run. Lasso is the genuine first, and arguably most elegant, specific technique in that family, a form of regularization that genuinely drives certain feature coefficients all the way to exactly zero during training itself, automatically excluding those features with no separate selection step required at all.

This topic covers the L1 penalty term Lasso genuinely adds to a model loss function, the real, genuine property that makes some coefficients land at exactly zero rather than just shrinking toward it, why a zero coefficient genuinely means a feature is fully excluded, how the alpha parameter genuinely controls how aggressive that selection becomes, and a real, practical requirement, features genuinely need to be scaled first for this technique to work fairly.
1. The L1 Penalty Term
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443422149-754692398.png

Lasso genuinely adds a penalty term directly to a model original loss function during training, alpha, a chosen strength parameter, multiplied by the genuine sum of the absolute values of every feature coefficient. This penalty genuinely discourages the model from assigning large coefficients to features, unless doing so meaningfully improves its real, actual predictions enough to outweigh that penalty cost.

This is genuinely the full mathematical idea behind Lasso, the acronym itself, Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator, directly describes this exact mechanism, shrinking coefficients using the absolute value penalty, which, as covered next, genuinely leads to real, automatic feature selection as a direct side effect.
2. Why Coefficients Genuinely Reach Exactly Zero

blocks.alt: Why Coefficients Genuinely Reach Exactly Zero
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443422374-839886731.png

The L1 penalty Lasso uses has a genuinely special mathematical property, the absolute value function real geometry, that causes some feature coefficients to land at precisely zero during training, not just shrink toward a small, nonzero value. This stands in genuine, direct contrast to L2 regularization, used by a closely related technique called Ridge, which shrinks coefficients toward zero but genuinely, almost never reaches exactly zero for any of them.

This exact zero property is genuinely the entire reason Lasso functions as a feature selection technique at all, and not merely a way to make coefficients smaller, exactly zero is a real, qualitative difference from merely small, one that genuinely, completely removes a feature influence rather than just reducing it.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: The genuine difference between Lasso and Ridge is not just a stylistic detail, it is the entire reason Lasso performs real feature selection while Ridge, covered briefly for contrast, genuinely does not.

blocks.text: 3. A Zero Coefficient Means Genuine Exclusion

blocks.alt: A Zero Coefficient Means Genuine Exclusion
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443422375-960041629.png

Once a feature genuine coefficient reaches exactly zero, that feature contributes genuinely nothing at all to the model final prediction, regardless of what value it actually holds for any given row. This is genuinely, functionally identical to that feature having been removed from the dataset entirely, even though it technically still sits in the input data.

This is exactly what makes Lasso a genuine embedded feature selection method, the selection did not require a separate step, computing scores beforehand or searching afterward, it genuinely happened automatically, as a direct, natural consequence of how the model itself was trained.
4. A Worked Example
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443422376-810269347.png
Fitting a Lasso model directly with scikit-learn shows this automatic exclusion happening in practice, on a small, familiar dataset.

code.content:
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import pandas as pd

X = pd.DataFrame({
    "square_feet": [900, 1200, 1500, 1800, 2100, 2400],
    "bedrooms": [2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5],
    "shoe_size_unrelated": [8, 9, 7, 10, 8, 9],
})
y = pd.Series([250000, 310000, 360000, 410000, 460000, 510000])

X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
model = Lasso(alpha=5000)
model.fit(X_scaled, y)

print(dict(zip(X.columns, model.coef_)))

blocks.text: With a genuinely strong enough alpha, shoe_size_unrelated genuine coefficient lands at exactly 0.0, automatically, genuinely excluded from the model without any separate feature selection step ever having been run.

blocks.title: A practical habit
blocks.content: Try a genuine range of alpha values, and check how many coefficients land at exactly zero for each. LassoCV, covered briefly in the Regression Algorithms module later, automates finding a genuinely well suited alpha directly.

blocks.text: 5. How Alpha Controls Selection Aggressiveness
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443422376-480688841.png

The alpha parameter genuinely controls how strong the L1 penalty actually is, a genuinely low alpha applies only a gentle penalty, letting most coefficients survive as small but nonzero values, while a genuinely high alpha applies a much stronger penalty, driving considerably more coefficients all the way to exactly zero, keeping only the genuinely most important features.

This makes alpha genuinely the single most important tuning decision when using Lasso specifically for feature selection, too low, and few features actually get excluded, too high, and genuinely useful features can get zeroed out along with the truly irrelevant ones, a real tradeoff covered in far more depth in the Hyperparameter Tuning module later in this course.

blocks.text: 6. The Real Requirement: Features Must Be Scaled First

blocks.alt: The Real Requirement: Features Must Be Scaled First
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443422377-950734648.png

Because the L1 penalty genuinely operates directly on raw coefficient magnitude, a feature measured on a genuinely large numeric scale would naturally need a genuinely smaller coefficient to have the same real effect on predictions as a feature on a genuinely small scale, making the penalty pressure unfairly uneven across features that have not been placed on a comparable footing first.

This is exactly why the worked example above applied StandardScaler, from the Feature Scaling module earlier in this course, before fitting Lasso, without that step, features with genuinely larger raw scales would be unfairly protected from the penalty, regardless of their real, actual importance to the target.
7. A Brief Contrast With Ridge
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785443422377-899231724.png

Ridge regression, a genuinely closely related technique using an L2 penalty instead, the sum of squared coefficients rather than absolute values, shrinks every coefficient toward zero but genuinely almost never reaches exactly zero for any of them. This means Ridge genuinely improves a model general stability and reduces overfitting, but it does not perform real feature selection the way Lasso genuinely does.

Both techniques are covered in far more complete depth in the Regression Algorithms module later in this course, this brief contrast here exists specifically to make clear why this particular topic focused on Lasso and its L1 penalty, and not Ridge, for the genuine feature selection use case this module is actually about.

blocks.text: 8. Lasso Versus What Comes Next

Lasso genuinely demonstrated the core embedded method idea concretely, feature selection emerging naturally from a single, regularized model training run, with zero coefficients directly identifying which features to drop. This technique, though, genuinely only applies to linear models specifically.

The next topic, Tree-Based Selection, covers a genuinely different embedded technique entirely, one built around decision trees and ensembles instead, where feature importance emerges naturally from how much each feature actually contributes to reducing error across every split in the tree, rather than from a coefficient penalty at all.

items: Lasso genuinely adds an L1 penalty, alpha times the sum of absolute coefficient values, to a model loss function.
This L1 penalty genuinely drives some feature coefficients all the way to exactly zero, unlike Ridge L2 penalty.
A genuine zero coefficient means that feature is functionally, effectively excluded from the model entirely.
The alpha parameter genuinely controls selection aggressiveness, low keeps more features, high excludes more.
Features genuinely must be scaled first, or the L1 penalty pressure becomes unfairly uneven across them.
The next topic, Tree-Based Selection, covers a genuinely different embedded technique, built around decision trees instead.
